analysis.one_liner: Bars federally insured banks and credit unions from speculative derivatives trading, allowing only regulator-approved hedging.
analysis.headline: Introduced with three Democratic sponsors in May 1994, the bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop banks and credit unions whose deposits are federally insured from buying and selling derivatives for their own profit. Derivatives are contracts whose value comes from other assets — bets on interest rates, currencies, or bond prices. Banks could still use them to hedge, meaning to offset risks they already have, but only if banking regulators approved. Any derivatives trading would have to move to a separately capitalized affiliate that is not itself an insured bank, and that affiliate would have to warn customers publicly that its losses are not covered by federal deposit insurance or by the parent company.
analysis.who_benefits: Depositors and taxpayers, whose FDIC-insured deposits would no longer sit behind risky derivatives trading; smaller banks that compete against big trading desks; and credit union members.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Deposit insurance, taxpayers, credit union members

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits insured depository institutions and their affiliates from any derivatives transaction for their own account, closing off trading risk backed by federal deposit insurance.

Allows hedging — transactions to offset risks on loans and investments the bank actually holds — only when approved by the federal banking agency, and requires banks to clearly identify each hedging transaction.
Permits derivatives only in affiliates that are separately capitalized from the insured bank, so losses there cannot drain the insured institution.
Requires affiliates to clearly and publicly notify customers that neither their assets nor the risk of loss from derivatives trades are federally insured or guaranteed by the parent company.
Applies the same prohibition to federally insured credit unions.

analysis.who_pays: Large banks and their trading affiliates, which would lose the ability to run derivatives positions with insured deposits behind them, and the derivatives dealers who sell those contracts to banks.

drawbacks.text: The hedging and de minimis exceptions are left almost entirely to regulators to define, so the practical reach of the ban depends on how strict the banking agencies write their rules.

Banks legitimately use derivatives to manage interest-rate and currency risk on real loans and deposits; a blanket ban with regulator-approved exceptions could make that risk management harder or slower, costs that could show up in lending rates.
A three-month wind-down for existing positions acknowledges the rule would force institutions to unwind existing derivatives positions, which can itself create losses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: keeping speculative derivatives away from insured deposits protects depositors and the FDIC fund, while the cost is some added friction for banks that use derivatives to hedge genuine risks. The bill tries to handle that with a hedging exception and separately capitalized affiliates, so an honest supporter could argue the costs are managed — though the exceptions lean heavily on regulators writing strict rules.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 1994 and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Sen. Byron Dorgan, joined by Sen. Barbara Mikulski, introduced the bill on May 17, 1994.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
That was the bill's final action; the committee never reported it and the full Senate never voted on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large banks and derivatives dealers were better off: nothing constrained derivatives trading at insured institutions, and the proposal to wall trading off from deposit insurance disappeared without ever being debated.

for.name: Sen. Byron Dorgan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Derivatives Limitations Act of 1994 and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sen. Barbara Mikulski
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as an original cosponsor.

for.name: 2 Senate Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill after its introduction.

against.name: Sen. Donald Riegle
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee and never advanced — no hearing, markup, or vote was scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat, but the bill never reached a vote, so the partisan shape of the full chamber is unknown.

industries.industry: Large banks and bank holding companies
industries.note: The bill would end their ability to trade derivatives for their own account using federally insured deposits, pushing any trading into separately capitalized affiliates. It preserves hedging only with regulator approval.

industries.industry: Derivatives dealers and swap dealers (investment banks)
industries.note: Insured banks are major buyers of swaps and other derivatives; removing them as customers would shrink the dealer market.
The bill applies the same derivatives ban to insured credit unions, though most credit unions did little derivatives trading, so the practical effect is small.
